title: Structure of Arabic Noun Forms
source: Original instructional lesson authored for this application (syllabus ref: Haywood & Nahmad Ch. 38; Ryding Ch. 5 §§5.1–5.7)
objectives: Distinguish primitive nouns (asmāʾ jāmidah) from derived nouns (mushtaqqāt).
Recognize common Form I maṣdar patterns (فَعْلٌ, فُعُولٌ, فِعَالَةٌ, فَعَالَةٌ).
Understand the nominal architecture of triliteral roots.
recallPrompt: From Chapter 20: Why are Form II–X maṣādir predictable while Form I maṣādir are lexical?

sections.heading: Primitive vs. Derived Nouns
sections.body: Classical Arabic grammarians divide nouns into primitive/underived nouns (asmāʾ jāmidah, such as رَجُلٌ 'man', شَمْسٌ 'sun', فَرَسٌ 'horse') and derived nouns (mushtaqqāt, such as participles, adjectives, and nouns of place/instrument) built on systematic morphological patterns.

sections.label: Common Form I Maṣdar Patterns
sections.summary: While Form I maṣādir must be verified in a dictionary, strong tendencies exist: فَعْلٌ (transitive verbs like ضَرْبٌ, فَتْحٌ), فُعُولٌ (intransitive motion like دُخُولٌ, خُرُوجٌ), and فِعَالَةٌ (crafts/professions like كِتَابَةٌ, تِجَارَةٌ).

sections.irab: طَلَبُ: مُبْتَدَأٌ مَرْفُوعٌ (مَصْدَرٌ وَهُوَ مُضَافٌ) | العِلْمِ: مُضَافٌ إِلَيْهِ مَجْرُورٌ | فَرِيضَةٌ: خَبَرٌ مَرْفُوعٌ
sections.notes: Notice how the maṣdar طَلَبُ functions as a noun ('the seeking of...').

sections.heading: Maṣādir Can Govern Objects
sections.body: In Classical Arabic, a maṣdar frequently takes a genitive muḍāf ilayh representing its logical object (طَلَبُ العِلْمِ 'seeking knowledge').
